title: Retirement
hookLine: a new season of service and prayer
tomorrow: why does a rumor need you to keep it alive?

cards: A sheet cake in the break room. A card signed by everyone, most of it saying relax, you've earned it. A last walk out to the car.
And then a quiet Monday, with nowhere to be by eight, and a question that can sneak up on anyone who worked a long time: so what am I for now? The card doesn't answer it. The question is old.

teach.h: CAST ME NOT OFF IN OLD AGE.
teach.b: One answer comes in an old person's own voice, in the Psalms. In the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Cast me not off in the time of old age: when my strength shall fail, do not thou forsake me."
Then the same psalm asks for time for one more job: to show God's strength to the generation that is to come. Old age with an assignment.
Luke shows it in Anna, a widow who never left the Temple, serving with fasting and prayer night and day, who saw the child Jesus and spoke of him to everyone who was waiting.

teach.h: A LIVING MEMORY TO PASS ON.
teach.b: Saint John Paul the Second wrote a letter to elderly people when he was old himself, and called them keepers of a living memory, with something to pass on.
Prayer, service, handing things down: a new season, not a closed door. A neighbor tradition gives this season a name.
In Hindu tradition, the Laws of Manu describe the stages of a life: when a householder sees his skin wrinkled, his hair white, and his children's children, he may turn toward the forest.
That stage is called vanaprastha, a life given more to prayer and less to getting.
Here Catholics and Hindus share a picture: the later years as a turn toward the spirit, not a slide into nothing. The difference is honest.
The classic Hindu stage steps back from household and town; the psalmist asks to stay right among the young, telling them.

how: In parishes, retired members often serve as lectors, visitors to the sick, catechists and people who pray for the parish; the Church celebrates a World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly in July.

games.q: your grandpa retired last month and keeps saying he's 'useless now.' your family wants to help. what fits today's lesson?
o: ask him to teach you the thing only he knows how to do.
tell him to relax; he's done being useful and earned it.
sign him up for enough activities that he's never bored.
games.why: the psalmist asks to stay long enough to tell the generation to come. the season changes; the handing-on begins.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has retired: a grandparent, a teacher, a coach, a neighbor. Send them one line naming something they handed down to you, a skill, a saying, a way of doing things.
Name it as specifically as you can: not thanks for everything, but the one thing. If you pray, you can hold them before God for a moment after it sends.

wordCard.voice: Retirement. The end of a working life, and in Catholic eyes the start of a season of prayer, service and handing on.

orig.note: Latin, Psalm 70:9 in the Vulgate: cast me not off, in the time of old age.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: a new season, like the psalmist asking for time to tell the young. Go gently.
